Collier, or "CJ" to his friends and family, is a dedicated fan of genre films - particularly science fiction, fantasy, and comic book adaptations, not to mention all forms of animation. This stems from a close bond with his father, who introduced him to these genres via copies of X-Men comics and reruns of the original Ultraman series. With his near-encyclopedic knowledge and bottomless love of genre, he's tackled a wide variety of articles.

Doctor Who is a show that has always managed to evolve, whether through the concept of "regeneration," which allows different actors to inhabit the mantle of the Doctor, or through recent revivals. Even now, the series is about to undergo another evolution, as the BBC has put it out to competitive tender in hopes that another production company will give it a modern refresh. However, the biggest change that Doctor Who made in 52 years happened during the Season 9 episode "Sleep No More," which put Peter Capaldi's Twelfth Doctor in the middle of a horror movie.

"Sleep No More" is shot in the style of a found-footage movie, with scientist Gagan Rassmussen (Reece Shearsmith) running into the Doctor and his companion Clara Oswald (Jenna Coleman) on the space station Le Verrier. Throughout the episode, the trio encounters "Sandmen," horrific creatures born from a machine Rassmussen created to alter how humans sleep. What makes "Sleep No More" stand out, beyond its unique point of view, is that it's the first episode of Doctor Who not to feature the series' signature title sequence. This heightens the horror, as viewers are thrust into the madness alongside the Doctor and Clara.
‘Doctor Who’ Delivers One of Its Most Terrifying Episodes in ‘Sleep No More’

blocks.c: Doctor Who Sleep No More

blocks.x: Every episode of Doctor Who usually follows a similar pattern: a short opening sequence establishes the time period, alien threat, or situation that the Doctor must solve, followed by the title sequence. "Sleep No More" changes this by starting with a video message from Rassmussen, following him as he explores Le Verrier and eventually encounters the Doctor. This means that for much of the episode, the Doctor isn't the main character. It immediately heightens the sense of dread, as viewers are thrown off guard by the Doctor's absence. Even the title card shifts, featuring an ominous string of numbers instead of the TARDIS flying through time and space.

This also makes "Sleep No More" one of the most terrifying episodes in the history of Doctor Who​​​​​​. The Sandmen are genuinely frightening, due to their misshapen bodies that are comprised of dust; they also kill their victims by slowly absorbing them into their sandy bodies. Considering that Doctor Who introduced nightmare fuel like the Weeping Angels and the Silence, that's saying a lot. However, the Sandmen's presence is nothing compared to the major twist in "Sleep No More," which throws the entire episode in a different light. At the end, the credits finally start rolling, but the dread remains.
